title: Night of the Living Dead
synopsis: A cemetery, a farmhouse, a basement argument, and a country radio voice that is finally telling the truth.

nodes.text: Three hours out of Pittsburgh to lay a wreath on a grave for a man neither of you can picture clearly. Johnny complains about the gas money, the radio, the drive back. Wind takes the flowers over twice. He does the voice from when you were nine, hands up, coming to get you, and you tell him to grow up. Behind him a man in a good suit is walking crooked between the stones.

choices.consequence: You give the voice straight back to him and he laughs, and that laugh is the last uncomplicated thing that happens to either of you.
You turn your back on him to fuss with the wreath wire, so you are facing entirely the wrong way when it matters.

nodes.text: Fifty yards off, in a suit and a tie, moving like a man with a stone in his shoe. You say excuse me. He does not answer. Closer, his mouth is working on nothing, and there is something wrong with the whites of his eyes, and his hands come up not to fend you off but to gather you in. He is astonishingly strong for an old man.

choices.consequence: You go to help, because he looked unwell, and you get near enough to smell him before your brother's arm comes across your chest.
You start for the car at once and leave Johnny standing there arguing with a stranger, which is exactly the sort of thing Johnny does.

nodes.text: They go over together into the gravel. Johnny's glasses skid away under a bench. His head meets the corner of a granite marker with a flat crack, and afterwards his legs keep moving for a while, and then they stop. The man in the suit gets up off him. Johnny does not. You are already at the car door with your fist on the handle and no keys anywhere.

choices.consequence: You put it in neutral and let gravity take you down the cemetery road, and you leave your brother lying in the gravel with a stranger.
You wait four seconds too long looking at the place where he is, and the rear window goes white with a rock.

nodes.text: The car goes off the road into a tree at the bottom of the hill and you run the last half mile. Porch light on, screen door hanging by one hinge, telephone with no dial tone. There is a pot on the stove boiled dry. Upstairs there is a smell you decide, for the moment, must be a dead animal in the wall.

choices.consequence: You go straight through the kitchen and put the bolt on behind you, and the smell upstairs waits patiently to introduce itself.
You crouch in the hedge by the gas pump for twenty minutes first, and count nine figures crossing the yard without any hurry at all.

nodes.text: Headlights, then a truck out of fuel, then a man in the doorway with a tire iron and his jacket over one arm. He asks whether you have been bitten. He says there is a rescue station with food and a radio fifteen miles up the county road. He is the calmest person you have met tonight, and he keeps talking while he works, because he can see what your face is doing.

choices.consequence: You hand him the lamp and hold the nails, and for two hours the house contains a working plan and two people who agree on it.
You sit on the stairs with your hands in your lap while he boards the windows alone, and he does not mention it once.

nodes.text: Every table, both interior doors, the banister, the front of a wardrobe, all of it goes over the glass in a lattice with three nails to a board. Hammering all night. What you are building is not a wall, it is a grille, and the whole point of a grille is that you can see out through it. Fingers come through the gaps while he is still measuring the next piece.

choices.consequence: You learn to hold a board flush against your own shaking, and by midnight your hands are steadier than your voice is.
You go up and sit on a stranger's bed under a wall of their photographs, and come down again only when the hammering stops.

nodes.text: Somebody has been under your feet the entire time. The cellar door opens on a middle-aged man in a good overcoat who has heard all of it, the shouting and the hammering and a girl crying in the kitchen, and stayed down there. He leads with an accusation so that he will not have to explain that. His wife and his daughter are on the steps behind him.

choices.consequence: You keep the argument in the doorway, and it emerges that Cooper has been waiting all night for somebody to be angry at.
You throw the bolt on your side and hear him start working at the wood immediately, and you have now made an enemy indoors.

nodes.text: The set on the mantel gets one station out of Pittsburgh. A man with a cold reads the wire copy in the voice they use for school closures: the recently dead are walking, they are feeding on the living, do not attempt to remove your dead yourselves. Then a list of rescue station towns, read twice, too fast. Then the part about the brain.

choices.consequence: You write the station towns on the wallpaper in pencil, and one of them turns out to be sixteen miles up the county road.
You cut it off mid-sentence because the girl in the corner has started shaking, and so you never hear the part about the trucks.

nodes.text: Cooper's daughter is on a bench in the cellar under her father's coat, grey-faced, with a bandage on her forearm from something that got her at the roadside. Her mother says she is cold. She asks for her mother in a small voice and then stops asking for anything at all. Nobody in this house will say the obvious thing aloud, and everybody in it has done the arithmetic.

choices.consequence: You take down water and a folded blanket and sit with Helen a while, and Helen thanks you, and the child's hand in yours is cold.
You stay up in the kitchen and let her family manage it, which costs you nothing tonight and everything by morning.

nodes.text: One door, one lock, no windows. Cooper says it the way a man closes a sale. Ben says a cellar is a hole you cannot see out of and cannot get out of, and asks what anybody eats on the third day. The two of them shout it out in a kitchen with a sick child underneath them and a radio giving out addresses neither man is now listening to.

choices.consequence: You side with the one who wants a way out, and Cooper takes it personally in a manner that has nothing to do with cellars.
You offer the cellar as a fallback and both men hear it as a defeat, and after that there are three separate plans in the house.

nodes.text: The teenagers come up shy, holding hands, apologising for not having come up sooner. Tom knows the farm. He knows the pump in the yard is padlocked and that the key hangs on the ring with the truck keys. Judy will not be left in the house without him and says so once, quietly. They are nineteen and twenty and they check each other's face before answering anything.

choices.consequence: You get all four of you round the table with a scrap of envelope and draw the yard, and for ten minutes it is a plan and not a hope.
You and Ben settle it between yourselves, and Judy is out the truck door and running across the dirt before anyone has told her the route.

nodes.text: The pump stands forty yards out across open ground and the tank is padlocked, which means the truck has to come to the pump and the key has to come off the ring on the wall. There are more of them in the yard every hour now, standing about unbothered, like people waiting for a bus. Ben sets light to a table leg and hands one to each of you.

choices.consequence: You take the torch and go, and the fire keeps them off you the entire way, and the entire way you are aware of your own back.
You let the boy drive because he knows the truck, and you watch Judy climb up beside him and pull the door shut after her.

nodes.text: The nozzle jumps out of the filler. Fuel goes over the sill of the truck door, down the panel, and out across the dirt in a shining line that runs all the way back to the pump. Everybody sees it. Everybody sees the burning table leg in somebody's hand, and the distance between those two things, and everybody thinks about it for roughly half a second.

choices.consequence: You send it out into the field, high and away, and it lands short in the grass, and the grass has not had rain in a month.
You let it fall at your feet, which is the one place you already knew there was gasoline, and the truck is already rolling.

nodes.text: The truck goes up with a soft thump you feel in your chest and rolls twenty feet before it stops against the fence. Judy's jacket is caught in the door handle. From the porch it is very bright and quite far away and there is nothing whatever to be done about it. The ones in the yard turn toward the light and walk to it, and in the morning there is very little left by the fence.

choices.consequence: You put your back to the window and listen instead, and listening turns out not to be the softer of the two options.
You stay at the boards and watch it through to the end, and you can name what they take, and you will keep that list.

nodes.text: The fire in the yard drew every one of them and then went out. Now they are at the house. Hands come through the lattice up to the elbow and take hold of the boards from the inside, and there are enough of them out there to pull together. A face arrives between two planks. Ben is hammering and firing and hammering again, and there is no furniture left.

choices.consequence: You put a match to the drapes and shove the whole burning bundle out through the gap, and it buys the front room four minutes.
You get a shoulder to the boards and your heels against the floor and hold, and you can feel individual fingers working through the wood.

nodes.text: The cellar door is standing open. She is at the bottom of the stairs in her nightdress with a mason's trowel off the workbench in one hand, and she has grown into the front of the house out of nowhere. Her mother's voice comes up from below, saying the child's name over and over, in a register you have never heard an adult use before.

choices.consequence: You get between the child and the doorway and find that you cannot make your arms do the necessary thing, and the moment goes past you.
You get out of the hall and put a door between yourself and a nine-year-old, and you will be defending that to yourself for fifty years.

nodes.text: Helen is down on the concrete by the workbench with the trowel coming down and she does not fight it, not with her hands and not with her voice. She says the child's name. Then she says it again with a question in it. The light down there is one bulb on a cord and the cord has been knocked, so the shadows on the wall keep changing size.

choices.consequence: You go three steps down and the door swings shut behind you, and after that it is dark, and after that you go back up.
You shoot the bolt with a woman still talking on the other side of it, and the talking becomes something else, and your hand stays on the bolt.

nodes.text: Cooper gets the rifle off Ben in the middle of the front room with the boards coming in, and cannot work the bolt, and fires it into the ceiling and then into a man's chest. Ben takes it back and puts two rounds into him at four feet, and by then it is not an accident and nobody pretends it is. Cooper crawls to the cellar door and lets himself down it.

choices.consequence: You get both hands on the barrel before it swings round again, and it takes all your weight, and it takes far too long.
You stand very still against the wall and let the two men settle it between them, and the settling is the loudest thing in the house.

nodes.text: Light comes up grey and the noise outside changes: dogs, engines, men calling to each other in flat county voices, a rifle every few seconds like fence posts being driven. The ones in the yard start drifting toward the treeline. Somebody out there laughs at something somebody else said. It is the ordinary sound of men doing a job on a Saturday, and it is coming closer.

choices.consequence: You get to the window and put a hand out through the gap, and a shape in a field takes half a second to decide what a hand is.
You stay low behind the boards and let them come at their own pace, and their pace is the pace of a hunting party.

nodes.text: The posse works a line through the corn with dogs on short leads. Their instruction is simple and has been repeated twice: anything upright in the yard, anything at a window, put it down and burn it after. Most of them are not police. They are men from the next township with their own rifles and coffee in a thermos, and they have had a very good morning.

choices.consequence: You shout from the front room and your voice comes out wrecked from a whole night of not screaming, and it does not carry past the porch.
You wait to be found rather than announce yourself, which is a reasonable decision made inside a house with no reasonable options left in it.

nodes.text: You come up the stairs at the sound of the engines and go to the glass, because the glass is where the light is. Out at eighty yards a man drops to one knee and settles his elbow on it. He is in no hurry. He has the whole morning. Between the two of you there is a torn curtain, one pane of farmhouse window, and a single assumption.

choices.consequence: You take one pace back from the glass, go down, and walk out through the front door with both hands high and empty.
You start toward the light and something in you says no, and your feet carry you back down the hall to the cellar stairs instead.
There is another morning where nobody is at that window at all, because you were out on the county road two hours before first light.

nodes.text: You come out onto the boards with both hands over your head and stand in the yard while a man in a hunting jacket decides. He asks your name. You give it. He lowers the muzzle, calls you ma'am, and offers you coffee out of a flask, while behind him two men drag last night into a heap for the fire. The coffee is very good. Nobody in the yard asks a single question about what happened inside the house.

The bolt holds until noon. You sit in the dark with a man who despises you and hear the radio through the floorboards give the all clear in the same voice it used for the school closures. When they open the door the daylight is unbearable. For fifty years afterward you sleep with a lamp on, and it is not the yard you see, or the boards, or the men with the dogs. It is a nine-year-old on a stair, holding a garden tool.

You get the pump open at four in the morning while the yard is empty and take the truck out with the headlights off and the window down. Dirt road, then blacktop, then a state route with cars nosed into the shoulder and left. The radio gives out addresses, then hymns, then nothing at all. Behind you the dust hangs in the mirror a long while before it settles, and the country, for one hour, is quiet.
